chief_complaint: greasy yellow scales on eyebrows and scalp
hpi_details: A 23-year-old male presents to the clinic with greasy yellow scales on eyebrows and scalp. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
ideas: He thinks the greasy yellow scales on his eyebrows and scalp are an extreme case of dandruff brought on by college stress and cheap shampoo.
concerns: He is worried that his eyebrows will permanently fall out and that people he meets will think he has disgusting personal hygiene.
expectations: He hopes to receive a powerful prescription shampoo or ointment that will wipe out the yellow crust before his upcoming date.

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Seborrheic Dermatitis (face) is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management emphasizes Plan for Seborrheic Dermatitis face: Ketoconazole 2% shampoo/cream, hydrocortisone cream, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.

common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Seborrheic Dermatitis (face).
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Psoriasis without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: New, severe, or treatment-refractory seborrheic dermatitis in an adult — screen for HIV infection.

boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective:
Chief Complaint: greasy yellow scales on eyebrows and scalp

A 23-year-old male presents with greasy, yellow, flaking scales localized to the eyebrows and scalp that have been gradually worsening.
reference_soap.objective: Ill-defined erythematous patches with greasy, yellow-white scale over the eyebrows, glabella, and scalp margins. No hair loss, pustules, or signs of secondary infection noted.
reference_soap.plan: Prescribe ketoconazole 2% shampoo used as a facial wash and a mild topical corticosteroid (e.g., hydrocortisone 1% cream) for inflamed areas. Advise regular use to control flares, as the condition is chronic and relapsing. Refer to dermatology if refractory to first-line therapy.

learning_objectives: Recognize clinical presentation and diagnostic markers of Seborrheic Dermatitis face
Select appropriate diagnostic workup for Seborrheic Dermatitis face
Implement evidence-based management plan: Ketoconazole 2% shampoo/cream, hydrocortisone cream

teaching.one_liner: A Malassezia-related inflammatory condition causing greasy yellow scaling on the eyebrows and scalp.
red_flags: New, severe, or treatment-refractory seborrheic dermatitis in an adult — screen for HIV infection
Signs of secondary bacterial or fungal superinfection (oozing, pain, spreading redness, fever)

must_ask.say: Is the scale greasy and yellow?
How long has this been going on?

history.answer: I've developed these greasy yellow flakes on my eyebrows and scalp that have been getting worse, and I've also been feeling quite tired lately.
It started about three weeks ago with some mild flaking on my scalp, and over the past week it spread to my eyebrows and got thicker.
It is strictly on my scalp, along my hairline, and over my eyebrows and the bridge between them; nowhere else on my face, chest, or body.
They look like reddish patches covered with yellowish, greasy flakes and dandruff. There are no blisters, pus bumps, or thick crusts.
The flakes feel soft, slightly oily, and greasy to the touch, clumping together rather than flaking off like dry silvery scales.
It itches mildly, especially when I get sweaty or warm, but there is no burning sensation or pain.
No, they stay in the exact same spots constantly. They do not fade and reappear after a few hours like hives.
I had mild dandruff a few times during high school exam periods, but it never appeared on my face before and regular shampoo took care of it back then.
I tried washing my hair and face more vigorously with my regular cleanser and applied a standard facial moisturizer, but it didn't help.
I haven't used any medicated ointments, steroid creams, or antifungal creams yet.
I've been staying up very late studying for university exams and feeling exhausted, which seems to trigger and worsen the flaking and redness.
No fever, chills, or generalized body aches at all, just feeling run-down and fatigued from lack of sleep.
No sores, blisters, or ulcers in my mouth, eyes, or genital area.
No, my skin is not peeling off, there is no skin pain, and I have no purple spots or bruises.
No swelling of my lips, tongue, or face, and no tightness in my chest, shortness of breath, or dizziness.
I haven't started or taken any new prescription drugs, antibiotics, pain relievers, or anti-gout medications.
I haven't changed my face wash, shampoo, cologne, or laundry detergent, and I haven't handled any plants or new metal accessories.
No one in my family, dorm, or friend circle has similar rashes or flaking skin.
No insect or tick bites, no outdoor hiking, no recent travel, and I haven't used any public baths or fitness centers.
I have never had atopic dermatitis, eczema, asthma, or allergic rhinitis.
No joint pain, morning stiffness, or swelling, and my fingernails look normal without any pits or ridges.
I have not had any new sexual partners or high-risk sexual contacts, and I have no history of genital ulcers or sores.
I thought it was just really severe dandruff that spread to my face because I've been stressed out and using cheap hair products.
I'm really worried that my eyebrow hair is going to fall out and that girls I meet will think I'm dirty and don't shower.
I have no chronic medical conditions such as hypertension, diabetes, or immune deficiencies.
I have never had any surgeries and have never been hospitalized.
I am not taking any regular medications, vitamins, or dietary supplements, and I have no known drug allergies.
I do not smoke and have never smoked cigarettes.
I am a social drinker and only have a glass or two of beer occasionally with friends.
I am a 23-year-old college student living in a university dormitory.
My father has mild dandruff, but no one in my family has psoriasis, eczema, or autoimmune conditions.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 118/76 mmHg, heart rate 72 beats/min, respiratory rate 14 breaths/min, body temperature 36.6 C, oxygen saturation 99% on room air.
Young male in no acute distress, alert and oriented, with visible yellowish flaking over the eyebrows and frontal hairline.
Ill-defined erythematous patches with greasy, yellow-white scale over the eyebrows, glabella, and scalp margins; no hair loss, pustules, crusting, or plaque induration on trunk or extremities.
Conjunctivae and sclerae are clear without erythema, discharge, or lid swelling.
Oral mucosa, lips, and posterior pharynx are pink and moist without aphthae, ulcers, or thrush.
No palpable lymphadenopathy in the anterior cervical, posterior cervical, or occipital chains.
No tenderness, swelling, or redness in hand or knee joints; fingernails show no pitting, discoloration, or onycholysis.
No rashes, ulcers, chancres, or weeping lesions on the external genitalia.
